power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Unpacking the Popularity of Online Peer Mental Health Support Groups in Menopause

text.text: This study connects research on the mental health threats of menopause with research on the effectiveness of online peer support for mental health challenges.
Online peer support groups are popular amongst menopausal women, yet the role such groups plays in supporting their psychological well-being has not previously been studied.

We used qualitative exploratory research methodology to collate and analyse the experiences of perimenopausal, menopausal, or post-menopausal women who used Facebook to access online peer groups for menopause support.
Group members with mental health challenges completed a short questionnaire about their mental health, menopause experiences, and uses/experiences of the group.

Participants identified ways in which the group had helped them and positive feelings which had arisen through group use, which had the potential to reduce negative feelings and mental health symptoms experienced during menopause.

Additionally, women identified negative impacts of the groups -so they are not a panacea, but should be prominent in the toolbox both for medical professionals and organizations concerned with signposting employees to appropriate support services, given that they are free and easy to access.
Furthermore, online peer support via free social media platforms has low access barriers for those with internet (Statista, 2023).
text.formatted: Furthermore, online peer support via free social media platforms has low access barriers for those with internet <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Statista, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: However, there has been little research specifically concerning the effectiveness and potential risks and benefits of online peer support for menopause provided through social media platforms (Rayland & Andrews, 2023).
text.formatted: However, there has been little research specifically concerning the effectiveness and potential risks and benefits of online peer support for menopause provided through social media platforms <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Rayland & Andrews, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Given that online resources play a significant part in the way menopausal women gain information on managing psychosocial symptoms of menopause, menopausal women's uses and outcomes in this area are under-researched (Cronin et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Given that online resources play a significant part in the way menopausal women gain information on managing psychosocial symptoms of menopause, menopausal women's uses and outcomes in this area are under-researched <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cronin et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Here, therefore, we explore what role peer support groups play in supporting the mental well-being of menopausal women who have mental health challenges (that is, a combination of stigmatizing conditions; O'Reilly et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Here, therefore, we explore what role peer support groups play in supporting the mental well-being of menopausal women who have mental health challenges (that is, a combination of stigmatizing conditions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">O'Reilly et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We also probed for possible risks that counterbalance these benefits, as scattered negative reports (misinformation, hostile comments, etc.) have emerged in prior research (Naslund et al., 2016).
text.formatted: We also probed for possible risks that counterbalance these benefits, as scattered negative reports (misinformation, hostile comments, etc.) have emerged in prior research <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Naslund et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: We explored the role that online peer support groups aimed specifically at menopausal women play in supporting those with mental health symptoms.
Participants (n=88) were recruited through four Facebook groups 2 whose administrators had agreed in advance to an anonymous Qualtrics questionnaire link being shared with their members.
Participants were required to be anatomically female and to have experienced mental health symptoms, whether diagnosed or undiagnosed.

The sample was diverse in age (26-63 years; M = 57) and other demographic variables; most reported residing in the UK, had been a member for more than a year, and were frequent and active users of the group (see supplementary materials).
2 When asked what menopause support group they belonged to, women mentioned numerous groups in addition to the groups from which they were recruited.
We focus on how women's use of the groups relates to (or addresses) the mental health and other menopause-related problems they perceive in their lives.
Due to the lack of research in this area, we used an exploratory research methodology.

Questionnaires allow researchers to gain access to a more diverse range of perspectives, including those who may choose to refuse to participate in face-to-face research because of the sensitivity of the topic (Braun et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Questionnaires allow researchers to gain access to a more diverse range of perspectives, including those who may choose to refuse to participate in face-to-face research because of the sensitivity of the topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Braun et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: After reading full details of the study and providing informed consent, participants completed a short questionnaire consisting of questions about their use of the group, about their mental health, and about how the group relates to it, followed by several demographic questions and a debriefing (see supplementary materials for question wordings).
Free text boxes enabled detailed responses.

After assigning pseudonyms, the first author used NVivo to sort and code the qualitative data using thematic analysis, a process which 'minimally organizes and describes your data set in (rich) detail' (Braun & Clarke, 2006, p.79).
text.formatted: After assigning pseudonyms, the first author used NVivo to sort and code the qualitative data using thematic analysis, a process which 'minimally organizes and describes your data set in (rich) detail' <ref type="bibr">(Braun & Clarke, 2006, p.79)</ref>.

text.text: The second and third authors consulted on a final set of themes.
An inductive, data-driven approach was chosen due to the exploratory nature of the study.
We identified two main themes: first, the debilitating extent of menopause-linked problems, and second, the mixed impact of the group, as relating specifically to those problems.
The latter had several subthemes.
The first theme that emerged was the severe challenges menopause faced women with, including mental health conditions, physical and cognitive symptoms, and a wide range of negative feelings.
Many women referenced the mental health condition that made them eligible to participate in the study.
Some of these had been experienced prior to menopause, such as anxiety or depression.

The majority felt these had worsened ('got worse at the latter stages of perimenopause and into post menopause' -Sophie, 57), but it is also worth noting that some women spoke of an improvement in mental health, typically attributed to hormone replacement therapy (HRT; 'low mood definitely improved with oestrogen and testosterone' -Kirsty, 46).
Since peri/menopause, women also reported experiencing a range of new conditions and symptoms.
Natalie (53), for example, described developing 'terrible anxiety which prevented me from seeing family and friends'.
Many women reported losing their ability to cope with daily living activities, such as leaving the house and going to work.
Alison (52) described this as 'like I'm juggling balls and peri menopause will make me drop them all.'
For some women this had necessitated emergency mental health support: 'I had a break down last year was off work for 7 weeks' (Natasha, 56).
For Andrea (50) the symptoms she experienced during perimenopause had particularly severe consequences: 'I didn't want to be here anymore.
I left my husband and young child when at my lowest point as I didn't trust myself not to hurt someone or myself.'
Separate from mental health conditions, participants also described physical and cognitive symptoms that they attributed specifically to menopause.
Physical symptoms included pain or tiredness -'I was desperately unwell in perimenopause' (Natalie, 53); 'aches [and] pains, missed heartbeats' (Ruth, 39); and 'joint stiffness' (Anne, 57).
text.formatted: Physical symptoms included pain or tiredness -'I was desperately unwell in perimenopause' (Natalie, 53); 'aches <ref type="bibr">[and]</ref> pains, missed heartbeats' (Ruth, 39); and 'joint stiffness' (Anne, 57).

text.text: Women described feeling 'total exhaustion' (Sandra, 61) and 'extreme fatigue' (Kathryn, 56).
Tiredness also meant lack of motivation for Amanda (52), who 'felt lethargic, no drive at home or work.
Nothing excited me.'

Cognitive symptoms included brain fog, lack of concentration, loss of vocabulary and memory problems -'feeling like my brain isn't keeping up with activities' (Kate, 53) -which had affected their abilities, from completing 'everyday tasks' (Kathryn, 53) to inability to 'retain new information' (Jaqueline, 53) needed to do their job effectively.
Some women added that these cognitive issues exacerbated emotional ones: 'I can completely forget conversations I have had and that then causes more anxiety' (Michelle, 41).

Jacqueline (53) spoke of the impacts of cognitive effects of menopause on her work: 'At their worst I thought I would have to leave my new, high skilled job because I just couldn't learn the new processes effectively.'
Lastly, participants attributed a wide range of unpleasant or unhappy emotions and feelings to menopause.

They reported that it had affected 'self-worth and value' (Kirsty, 46) resulting in 'feelings of worthlessness' (Sandra, 61) and 'feeling useless' (Sharon, 54); 'self confidence is always low' (Elaine, 57).
Some women described feeling stressed: Karen (57) explained, 'even doing basic tasks like parking my car can now be overwhelming.'
Kathryn (56) described the 'rage and anger' she had experienced since menopause.
Others reported feeling overemotional.
Claire (26) describes feeling 'Increasingly insecure and teary.
I cry a lot more and have more self-doubt.'

A prominent negative feeling was women feeling as if they were going mad or crazy; Suzanne (45) stated she joined because she 'felt like I was losing my mind and desperately needed solidarity' and Kirsty (46) was seeking 'validation that I wasn't going insane.'
Cheryl (41) said: "It felt like I was going crazy and no one had an answer.'
Natalie (53) said that she felt entirely changed: 'my joy in life vanished and I became a shell of my former self.'

Notably, a subset of these comments specifically referenced that these negative feelings were triggered by or worsened by a lack of support from health care professionals, for example 'lack of knowledge' from GPs (Sandra, 61) meaning 'you have to do the research all yourself' (Natasha, 56) and medical professionals who 'don't understand or are not educated about the menopause' (Vanessa, 50).
Lorraine (49) describes that her doctor 'was no help at all'.
As participants described various roles that the group played in relation to the problems above, a mixed (although largely positive) portrait of the group's impact emerged.
First, consistent with past work on online peer support groups (Cecil et al., 2024), the group was described as providing various kinds of support, described below.
text.formatted: First, consistent with past work on online peer support groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Cecil et al., 2024)</ref>, the group was described as providing various kinds of support, described below.

text.text: Due to these supports, respondents identified a range of positive emotions and outcomes that they attributed to use of the group, some of which had potential to balance out their negative feelings around menopause and reduce the effect of mental health symptoms.
Ultimately, Christine (42) captured others' views in saying that 'the group has given me hope' and Natasha (56) similarly described it as 'a life saver.'

Many joined the group to gain basic knowledge about menopause and HRT ('It has helped me access important and useful information on the HRT treatments available and dosages' -Kerry, 46), including from menopause specialists in some cases.
Reliable information was described as scarce elsewhere ('there was little information that I felt I could trust' -Nichola, 54).
This had helped some in a practical way: "Bit by bit [...] things began to make a bit more sense and I knew what I had to fight for in terms of HRT" (Natalie, 43).
In addition to basic information-seeking, many wanted to connect with others and, in some cases, express the value of those connections with reciprocal information-sharing.
Tina (44) joined the group 'to speak with other women so that I didn't feel so alone and if possible help others by sharing my own experiences.'
Respondents described how the solidarity they felt as part of the group made them feel validated and empowered.

Women who had previously felt they were going 'insane' found the group helped 'normalise the [menopause] experience' (Lucy, 49), which facilitated symptom management ("knowing my experience is fairly normal amongst the women in the group has helped me worry less about my cognitive decline" -Sophie, 57).
They experimented with new coping strategies; ultimately, Kathryn (56) felt the group had 'improved the way I manage my own mental health.'

One of the most often-mentioned skills that women described developing was self-advocacy, and women explicitly used the language of "empowerment" to describe their newfound confidence since joining the group: 'It has helped me feel like I am not alone and empowered me to find resources and advocate for myself' (Kerry, 46).
text.formatted: One of the most often-mentioned skills that women described developing was self-advocacy, and women explicitly used the language of "empowerment" to describe their newfound confidence since joining the group: 'It has helped me feel like I am not alone and empowered me to find resources and advocate for myself' <ref type="bibr">(Kerry,</ref> <ref type="bibr">46)</ref>.

text.text: 'It's empowering to read others' views and experiences and gives me the confidence to challenge medical professionals when needed' (Michelle, 41).

Sophie (57) was one of several participants who directly connected the validating interactions she experienced within the group to her changed behavior outside the group: "I have felt less freakish and I now consider my symptoms quite normal.
As a result I feel less alone, less scared that I'm not going mad and more able to stand up for myself when dealing with the medical profession, which has felt like a constant battle."
A smaller number of women talked about harmful or detrimental effects of the group.
A negative for Cheryl (41) was the feeling of over-reliance on the group; she felt 'it can become a crutch.'
Some noted that posts tended to focus on the negative experiences, which Michelle (41) said resulted in her 'overthinking symptoms' and Claire (26) suggested 'provides a skewed picture of menopause'.
This resulted in Claire feeling 'scared' after reading how others going through menopause had experienced relationship breakdowns, loss of employment, and suicidal feelings.
Jennifer (53) said: 'Reading the awful things people were going through made me fear for my future.'

Kelly (48) found reading 'some people's comments about taking years to find the right combination' made her worry about getting the right treatment and Melanie ( 56) described how she 'ended up having to avoid reading other people's experiences' during a health scare 'because it increased my anxiety levels.'
text.formatted: Kelly (48) found reading 'some people's comments about taking years to find the right combination' made her worry about getting the right treatment and Melanie ( <ref type="formula">56</ref>) described how she 'ended up having to avoid reading other people's experiences' during a health scare 'because it increased my anxiety levels.'

text.text: Some women felt despondent for others who were suffering: 'It has saddened me to hear just how common it is to not get the support and correct advice from health care professionals and just how widespread lack of menopause knowledge still is' (Melanie, 56).
Thus, for some women the sharing of experiences could act as a trigger for anxiety or sadness.
Additionally, some women said they had witnessed incorrect advice ('there is a lot of misinformation out there' -Teresa, 57) or even bullying ('women being mean to other women' -Ruth, 39).
While positive impacts of the group can counteract some of the debilitating challenges of menopause, negative impacts have the potential to worsen distress instead of alleviating it.
This study connects two research areas: one on the effectiveness of online peer support for those with mental health challenges, and the other on the mental health of menopausal women.

We found that participants reported mixed, though on balance largely positive, experiences and functions of using online peer support groups to manage mental health conditions and other distressing symptoms and feelings linked to menopause.

For example, giving and receiving support equipped group members to better manage their mental health symptoms, and women's sense of connectedness with others in the group (cf. Hayfield et al., 2024; Cecil et al., 2024) led to feeling validated and the normalisation of shared experiences.
text.formatted: For example, giving and receiving support equipped group members to better manage their mental health symptoms, and women's sense of connectedness with others in the group (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Hayfield et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Cecil et al., 2024)</ref> led to feeling validated and the normalisation of shared experiences.

text.text: This aligns with past work on how such groups support those with mental health problems -even severe ones (Naslund, 2016; Sun et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This aligns with past work on how such groups support those with mental health problems -even severe ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Naslund, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Sun et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, benefits have the potential to extend beyond the group and its members.

There has been increased cultural interest in menopause over recent years and more effort than ever is being made to increase public awareness around the topic (Hickey et al., 2022; Rees et al., 2021).
text.formatted: There has been increased cultural interest in menopause over recent years and more effort than ever is being made to increase public awareness around the topic <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Hickey et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Rees et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Despite this, >80% of respondents to a national survey of peri/menopausal women (Dahlgren et al., 2023) reported feeling stigma associated with their menopause symptoms, and women often feel that they should 'suffer in silence' ( O'Reilly et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite this, >80% of respondents to a national survey of peri/menopausal women <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Dahlgren et al., 2023)</ref> reported feeling stigma associated with their menopause symptoms, and women often feel that they should 'suffer in silence' ( <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">O'Reilly et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings suggest that online peer support groups can help reduce shame, bolster confidence, and empower women to combat social stigma (Schaedel & Ryder, 2022); as Alexandra (49) commented: 'The menopause is still taboo in a lot of areas and this group is certainly spreading the word.'
text.formatted: Our findings suggest that online peer support groups can help reduce shame, bolster confidence, and empower women to combat social stigma <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Schaedel & Ryder, 2022)</ref>; as Alexandra (49) commented: 'The menopause is still taboo in a lot of areas and this group is certainly spreading the word.'

text.text: These are precisely the optimal intervention 'ingredients' called for by researchers studying mental health challenges during menopause (Sergeant & Rizq, 2017).
text.formatted: These are precisely the optimal intervention 'ingredients' called for by researchers studying mental health challenges during menopause <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Sergeant & Rizq, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: One of the most interesting observations to emerge from this study was the contrast between perceptions of medical professionals (seen as unhelpful, inaccessible or rushed, and a source of stigma and shame) and perceptions of the online peer group (generally seen as empowering and validating, as well as being easy to access) -helping to illuminate why increasingly peri/menopausal women may be turning to online peer groups as a preferred source of support (ABC News, 2018).

As in previous research (Naslund et al., 2016), this study also highlighted potential risks of online peer support groups such as misinformation and potential to increase anxiety -given this, it's all the more pressing to understand the perceived benefits that prompt women to use online peer support groups in ever-increasing numbers.
text.formatted: As in previous research <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Naslund et al., 2016)</ref>, this study also highlighted potential risks of online peer support groups such as misinformation and potential to increase anxiety -given this, it's all the more pressing to understand the perceived benefits that prompt women to use online peer support groups in ever-increasing numbers.

text.text: One strength of this study is its novelty: though some have called for using technology to greater effect in the menopause space (Cronin et al., 2020) this is the first study we are aware of to investigate online peer support aimed specifically at menopausal women, despite the obvious popularity of this approach amongst those women.
text.formatted: One strength of this study is its novelty: though some have called for using technology to greater effect in the menopause space <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Cronin et al., 2020)</ref> this is the first study we are aware of to investigate online peer support aimed specifically at menopausal women, despite the obvious popularity of this approach amongst those women.

text.text: A second strength is the applicability of self-advocacy as a pathway for worldwide cultural change (via stigma reduction).
All responses were self-reported, and the sample consisted of active userspredominantly British -of a small number of Facebook groups, so generalizability needs further attention.

Granting these limitations, since online peer groups for menopause support already exist and are generally free to access, if women feel unsupported in "formal" structures --such as by their employers and GPs --reputable ones are an effective and economical place to direct menopausal women.
